questions.title: How Database Indexes Work Internally
questions.question: How does a B-tree index work internally and how does the database use it to answer queries faster?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- B-tree: balanced tree with sorted keys and pointers to heap (table) pages
- O(log n) lookups vs O(n) sequential scan
- Leaf nodes linked for efficient range scans
- Index entry points to physical row location (heap tuple)
- Write overhead: every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE must update all indexes
- Page splits: when a B-tree node is full, it splits — causes index bloat
- VACUUM/AUTOVACUUM in PostgreSQL reclaims dead tuple space from the index too

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
A B-tree index is a balanced tree of sorted values where each leaf node holds the indexed column value and a pointer to the actual row in the table. The tree is kept balanced so that every lookup takes the same number of steps, giving O(log n) performance. For a table with a million rows, that's roughly 20 comparisons versus a million for a sequential scan.

Leaf nodes in a B-tree are linked to each other in order. This is what makes range queries efficient — once the index finds the first matching value, it can walk the leaf nodes sequentially to collect the rest of the range without going back to the root.

The cost of having an index is write performance. Every INSERT must add an entry to every index on that table. Every DELETE must remove from every index. UPDATE is effectively a delete plus insert in each index. A heavily indexed table can be two to five times slower for writes. This is why you index only what your actual query patterns require.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## B-tree Structure (Conceptual)

```
                    [50]
                   /    \
              [25]        [75]
             /    \      /    \
         [10,20] [30,40] [60,70] [80,90]
          ↓  ↓    ↓  ↓    ↓  ↓    ↓  ↓
        Row Row  Row Row  Row Row  Row Row
        Ptrs     Ptrs     Ptrs     Ptrs
```

Leaf nodes are linked: [10,20] → [30,40] → [60,70] → allows range scan without going to root

## Index Scan vs Sequential Scan

```sql
-- Small result set → index scan (log n lookups)
SELECT * FROM employees WHERE id = 12345;  -- single row, index wins

-- Large result set → seq scan might be cheaper
SELECT * FROM employees WHERE salary > 1;  -- 99% of rows, skip index overhead
-- Optimizer picks seq scan here — reading all pages is faster than jumping around
```

## Index Bloat and Maintenance

```sql
-- Check index size vs table size
SELECT indexname,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(indexrelid)) AS index_size
FROM pg_stat_user_indexes
WHERE relname = 'orders'
ORDER BY pg_relation_size(indexrelid) DESC;

-- Rebuild bloated index without locking (PostgreSQL)
REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_customer_id;

-- Check bloat from dead tuples
SELECT relname, n_dead_tup, n_live_tup
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
WHERE n_dead_tup > 1000;
```

## Hash Index — Equality Only

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_email_hash ON users USING HASH (email);
-- Faster equality lookup: WHERE email = 'foo@bar.com'
-- Cannot do range: WHERE email LIKE 'foo%' → fails
-- Cannot sort: ORDER BY email → cannot use this index
```

speakable_v2.hook: A B-tree index is a balanced tree of sorted values where each leaf node holds the indexed column value and a pointer to the actual row in the table.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: This is why you index only what your actual query patterns require.

questions.title: Reading and Using EXPLAIN ANALYZE
questions.question: How do you use EXPLAIN ANALYZE to identify and fix slow queries?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- EXPLAIN shows planned operations; ANALYZE adds actual execution stats
- BUFFERS shows how many disk pages were read (cache hits vs reads)
- Seq Scan on large table = likely missing index
- High filter rows removed = index selectivity problem
- Nested Loop with large outer table = missing index on inner table
- Hash Join: good for large tables; Merge Join: good for pre-sorted data
- Rows estimated vs actual: large discrepancy = stale table statistics (run ANALYZE)

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
EXPLAIN shows you the query plan the database intends to execute — which tables it will scan, in what order, and what join algorithms it'll use. Adding ANALYZE actually runs the query and collects real execution statistics. Adding BUFFERS shows you how many disk pages were read and how many came from cache.

The key things to look for are sequential scans on large tables, which almost always indicate a missing index. Look at the cost estimates — the final node's estimated cost tells you what the planner thinks the query will cost. If actual rows are dramatically different from estimated rows, your table statistics are stale and you should run ANALYZE on the table so the planner makes better decisions.

Nested loop joins are efficient for small inner tables but terrible when both sides are large and the inner table isn't indexed. If you see a nested loop with a large outer row count and a seq scan inside, the fix is almost always to add an index on the join column of the inner table.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## EXPLAIN ANALYZE Output

```sql
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, FORMAT TEXT)
SELECT o.*, c.name
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.status = 'pending';

-- Sample output:
-- Hash Join  (cost=125.50..3210.75 rows=842 width=312)
--             (actual time=15.241..102.334 rows=856 loops=1)
--   Buffers: shared hit=892 read=312
--   -> Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0..2800 rows=842 width=280)
--       Filter: (status = 'pending')
--       Rows Removed by Filter: 52000   ← 52k rows scanned, 856 useful
--   -> Hash  (cost=80..80 rows=3640 width=32)
--       -> Seq Scan on customers  (cost=0..80 rows=3640 width=32)
```

**Key observations from this plan:**
- 52,000 rows scanned to find 856 → add index on `status`
- Buffers: `read=312` means 312 pages came from disk, not cache → I/O intensive

```sql
-- Fix: add partial index (only pending orders)
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_pending ON orders (customer_id, created_at)
WHERE status = 'pending';
```

## Join Algorithm Guide

| Algorithm | Best For |
|-----------|-----------|
| Nested Loop | Small inner table with index |
| Hash Join | Large tables, no sort order needed |
| Merge Join | Both sides pre-sorted on join key |

## Update Statistics

```sql
-- Stale stats = bad estimates = bad plans
ANALYZE orders;          -- update table stats
ANALYZE;                 -- update all tables
VACUUM ANALYZE orders;   -- reclaim space AND update stats
```

speakable_v2.hook: EXPLAIN shows you the query plan the database intends to execute — which tables it will scan, in what order, and what join algorithms it'll use.
speakable_v2.cap: If you see a nested loop with a large outer row count and a seq scan inside, the fix is almost always to add an index on the join column of the inner table.

questions.title: Composite vs Single Column Indexes
questions.question: How do composite indexes differ from single-column indexes, and how do you decide the column order?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Composite index covers queries involving multiple columns in the index
- Leftmost prefix rule: index on (A,B,C) can satisfy queries on A, A+B, or A+B+C — not B alone
- Put the most selective column first? Not always — put the equality column first, range column last
- Equality before range: WHERE dept='Eng' AND salary > 80000 → index on (dept, salary)
- Covering index: include all query columns to avoid heap lookup (Index-Only Scan)
- More indexes = more write overhead — find the right balance

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
A composite index covers multiple columns in a defined order. The leftmost prefix rule determines which queries can use it: an index on department, salary, hire_date can answer queries filtering on department, or on department and salary, but not on salary alone — because the sorted structure starts with department, not salary.

The order of columns in a composite index matters based on your query patterns. Put columns used in equality conditions before columns used in range conditions. If you have a query filtering WHERE department = 'Engineering' AND salary > 80000, put department first and salary second. The index can jump directly to all Engineering rows and then scan the salary range within that subset.

A covering index takes this further by including all columns the query needs, eliminating the need to look up the actual table row at all. When EXPLAIN shows an Index Only Scan, the query is being served entirely from the index — maximum efficiency.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Leftmost Prefix Rule

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_emp ON employees (department, salary, hire_date);

-- ✅ Uses index (starts with 'department')
WHERE department = 'Engineering';
WHERE department = 'Engineering' AND salary > 80000;
WHERE department = 'Engineering' AND salary > 80000 AND hire_date > '2022-01-01';

-- ❌ Cannot use this index (no leading column)
WHERE salary > 80000;
WHERE hire_date > '2022-01-01';

-- ❌ Only partially uses index (range breaks prefix chain)
WHERE department LIKE 'Eng%' AND salary > 80000;  -- range on dept, salary part skipped
```

## Equality Before Range

```sql
-- Query: WHERE status = 'active' AND created_at > '2024-01-01'

-- GOOD: equality column first, range column second
CREATE INDEX idx_good ON orders (status, created_at);
-- → Jumps to all 'active' rows, then range scans created_at within that

-- NOT AS GOOD: range first
CREATE INDEX idx_bad ON orders (created_at, status);
-- → Scans from 2024-01-01 forward and filters status separately
```

## Covering Index — Index Only Scan

```sql
-- Query needs: department, name, salary (no other columns)
SELECT name, salary FROM employees
WHERE department = 'Engineering'
ORDER BY salary DESC;

-- Covering index: all needed columns included
CREATE INDEX idx_covering ON employees (department, salary DESC, name);
-- EXPLAIN now shows: Index Only Scan (no heap access) ← fastest possible
```

## When NOT to Use Composite Index

```sql
-- Low cardinality first column — wastes the index
CREATE INDEX bad ON orders (status, customer_id);
-- 'status' has 3 values (pending/active/done) — not selective enough as first column
-- Better: (customer_id, status) or separate indexes
```

speakable_v2.hook: A composite index covers multiple columns in a defined order.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: When EXPLAIN shows an Index Only Scan, the query is being served entirely from the index — maximum efficiency.

questions.title: Index Maintenance and Bloat
questions.question: How do database indexes get bloated and what should you do to maintain them in production?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Bloat: dead tuples from updates/deletes leave ghost entries in indexes
- AUTOVACUUM: PostgreSQL's background process that reclaims dead tuple space
- REINDEX: rebuilds index from scratch — compact but locks table (use CONCURRENTLY)
- Unused indexes: tracked in pg_stat_user_indexes — drop unused to save write overhead
- Monitor index size and usage regularly
- Hot table: high update rate → frequent vacuuming needed; tune autovacuum thresholds

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Indexes accumulate bloat over time because PostgreSQL uses multi-version concurrency control — when you update or delete a row, the old version isn't immediately removed. It stays in the table and in the index as a dead tuple, taking up space. AUTOVACUUM runs in the background to reclaim this space, but on high-traffic tables it might not keep up.

Bloated indexes are larger than necessary, which means more disk reads for every lookup and more memory needed to cache them. If an index grows to several times its necessary size, you'll see degraded query performance even though the index technically exists.

The other maintenance concern is unused indexes. Every index you have slows down writes. If an index isn't being used by any queries, it's pure overhead. PostgreSQL tracks index usage in system views, so you can identify and drop indexes that haven't been used since the server last restarted.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Check Index Bloat

```sql
-- Indexes with high dead tuple ratio
SELECT
    t.relname AS table_name,
    ix.indexrelid::regclass AS index_name,
    pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(ix.indexrelid)) AS size,
    s.idx_scan AS scans_since_restart
FROM pg_index ix
JOIN pg_stat_user_indexes s USING (indexrelid)
JOIN pg_stat_user_tables t ON t.relid = ix.indrelid
ORDER BY pg_relation_size(ix.indexrelid) DESC
LIMIT 20;
```

## Identify Unused Indexes

```sql
-- Indexes with zero scans since last server restart
SELECT schemaname, tablename, indexname, idx_scan
FROM pg_stat_user_indexes
WHERE idx_scan = 0
  AND NOT EXISTS (
      SELECT 1 FROM pg_constraint c
      WHERE c.conindid = indexrelid  -- keep PK and FK indexes
  )
ORDER BY pg_relation_size(indexrelid) DESC;

-- Drop unused index (always verify first)
DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_old_status;
```

## Rebuild Bloated Index

```sql
-- Non-concurrent: fast but locks table (avoid in prod during traffic)
REINDEX INDEX idx_orders_customer_id;

-- Concurrent: no lock, runs in background
REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_customer_id;
-- Creates new index alongside old, swaps atomically, drops old
```

## Tune Autovacuum for Hot Tables

```sql
-- Orders table updates frequently — vacuum more aggressively
ALTER TABLE orders SET (
    autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.01,   -- vacuum after 1% dead tuples (default 20%)
    autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor = 0.005  -- analyze after 0.5% changes
);
```

speakable_v2.hook: Indexes accumulate bloat over time because PostgreSQL uses multi-version concurrency control — when you update or delete a row, the old version isn't immediately removed.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: PostgreSQL tracks index usage in system views, so you can identify and drop indexes that haven't been used since the server last restarted.

questions.title: Diagnosing Slow Queries in Production
questions.question: How do you systematically find and diagnose slow queries in a production PostgreSQL database?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Enable pg_stat_statements to track query performance over time
- slow_query_log / log_min_duration_statement to capture long-running queries
- EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the captured query to get execution plan
- Check for lock waits: pg_locks + pg_stat_activity
- Connection pool exhaustion: max_connections limits, use PgBouncer
- Look at query_time, total_time, calls in pg_stat_statements to find top offenders
- Don't EXPLAIN on production under load — use a replica or staging clone

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The first step is knowing which queries are slow. Enable pg_stat_statements extension if it isn't already — it collects execution statistics for every unique query shape across all calls. Then sort by total execution time, not per-call time, because a query that takes one millisecond but runs a million times is a bigger problem than one that takes five seconds but runs once a day.

Once you have a candidate query, get the plan with EXPLAIN ANALYZE. But be careful — in production under load, EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes the query. Use a read replica or a recent clone of the database instead to avoid adding load during an incident.

Beyond slow queries, also check for lock contention. Long-running transactions that hold locks while other queries pile up waiting look like slow queries from the application's perspective but are actually a blocking problem. pg_stat_activity shows you currently running queries and their wait states.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Enable pg_stat_statements

```sql
-- In postgresql.conf:
-- shared_preload_libraries = 'pg_stat_statements'

-- After restart:
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_stat_statements;

-- Find top 10 slowest queries by total time
SELECT query,
       calls,
       total_exec_time::NUMERIC(12,2)     AS total_ms,
       mean_exec_time::NUMERIC(12,2)      AS avg_ms,
       stddev_exec_time::NUMERIC(12,2)    AS stddev_ms,
       rows
FROM pg_stat_statements
ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC
LIMIT 10;
```

## Log Slow Queries

```sql
-- Log queries taking over 1 second
ALTER SYSTEM SET log_min_duration_statement = '1000';  -- milliseconds
SELECT pg_reload_conf();
```

## Detect Lock Contention

```sql
-- Queries waiting for locks
SELECT blocking.pid                AS blocking_pid,
       blocking.query               AS blocking_query,
       blocked.pid                  AS blocked_pid,
       blocked.query                AS blocked_query,
       blocked.wait_event_type,
       blocked.wait_event
FROM pg_stat_activity blocked
JOIN pg_stat_activity blocking
     ON blocking.pid = ANY(pg_blocking_pids(blocked.pid))
WHERE blocked.wait_event_type = 'Lock';
```

## Quick Diagnosis Checklist

1. `pg_stat_statements` → top total_exec_time queries
2. `log_min_duration_statement` → capture actual slow query text
3. `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` on replica → find seq scans, nested loops
4. Check `pg_stat_activity` → any Lock wait events?
5. Check autovacuum: `pg_stat_user_tables` n_dead_tup column
6. Check connection count: are you hitting max_connections?

speakable_v2.hook: The first step is knowing which queries are slow.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: pg_stat_activity shows you currently running queries and their wait states.

questions.title: SQL Query Rewriting for Performance
questions.question: What are common query rewriting techniques to improve SQL performance without adding indexes?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Replace correlated subquery with JOIN or window function
- Replace NOT IN with NOT EXISTS (NULL-safe, often faster)
- Push filters into derived tables / CTEs to reduce rows early
- Avoid functions on indexed columns in WHERE — prevents index use
- Use EXISTS for existence checks instead of COUNT(*) > 0
- Avoid SELECT * — fetch only needed columns, especially with wide tables
- Batch large updates/deletes with LIMIT to avoid long-running locks

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
One of the most impactful query rewrites is eliminating correlated subqueries. A correlated subquery re-executes for every row in the outer result. Rewriting it as a JOIN or window function converts it from an O(n) inner loop to a single pass over the data.

Another common issue is wrapping indexed columns in function calls inside a WHERE clause. If you write WHERE UPPER(email) = 'TEST@EXAMPLE.COM', the index on the email column cannot be used — the function transforms every value and the database must scan every row. The fix is to store the data normalized, use a functional index on UPPER(email), or rewrite the query to avoid the function.

For existence checks, use EXISTS rather than COUNT(*) > 0. EXISTS stops as soon as it finds one matching row. COUNT(*) > 0 counts every single matching row and then checks if that number is greater than zero — pure wasted work.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Replace Correlated Subquery with JOIN

```sql
-- SLOW: correlated subquery runs once per employee row
SELECT name FROM employees e
WHERE salary > (
    SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees WHERE department = e.department
);

-- FAST: window function — single pass
SELECT name FROM (
    SELECT name, salary, AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department) AS dept_avg
    FROM employees
) t WHERE salary > dept_avg;
```

## Avoid Functions on Indexed Columns

```sql
-- SLOW: index on created_at cannot be used — YEAR() wraps every value
WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2024;

-- FAST: range condition — index can scan from start to end of 2024
WHERE created_at >= '2024-01-01' AND created_at < '2025-01-01';

-- SLOW: index on email is unused
WHERE LOWER(email) = 'test@example.com';

-- FAST option 1: functional index
CREATE INDEX idx_email_lower ON users (LOWER(email));
WHERE LOWER(email) = 'test@example.com';  -- now uses the functional index

-- FAST option 2: store normalized data
WHERE email = 'test@example.com';  -- normalize on write, don't transform on read
```

## EXISTS vs COUNT for Existence Check

```sql
-- SLOW: counts all matches
IF (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 123) > 0 THEN ...

-- FAST: stops at first match
IF EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 123) THEN ...
```

## Batch Large Updates

```sql
-- SLOW: one huge update holds a lock for seconds
UPDATE orders SET status = 'archived' WHERE created_at < '2022-01-01';

-- BETTER: batch processing — releases lock between batches
DO $$
BEGIN
    LOOP
        UPDATE orders SET status = 'archived'
        WHERE id IN (
            SELECT id FROM orders
            WHERE created_at < '2022-01-01' AND status != 'archived'
            LIMIT 1000
        );
        EXIT WHEN NOT FOUND;
        PERFORM pg_sleep(0.1);  -- brief pause to let other queries in
    END LOOP;
END $$;
```

speakable_v2.hook: One of the most impactful query rewrites is eliminating correlated subqueries.
speakable_v2.cap: COUNT() > 0 counts every single matching row and then checks if that number is greater than zero — pure wasted work.

questions.title: Table Partitioning for Large Tables
questions.question: What is table partitioning in PostgreSQL and when should you use it for large tables?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Partitioning: physically splitting one logical table into smaller physical child tables
- Partition pruning: queries that filter on partition key only scan relevant partitions
- Types: RANGE (dates), LIST (categories/statuses), HASH (even distribution)
- When to use: table above ~50-100GB, queries always filter on partition key, archival/deletion by range
- Local indexes on each partition, not global index across all partitions
- Trade-offs: more complex schema, cross-partition queries scan all partitions

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Partitioning splits one logical table into multiple physical child tables called partitions, each storing a subset of the data based on a partition key. The main benefit is partition pruning — when a query filters on the partition key, the database only reads the partitions that could contain matching data and completely ignores the rest.

The classic use case is time-series data like orders or events, partitioned by month or year. A query for orders in January 2024 only touches the January 2024 partition, which might be a few gigabytes out of a table that's hundreds of gigabytes total. This is dramatically faster than scanning an unpartitioned table and finding the same rows via an index.

Partitioning also makes data lifecycle management much easier. Dropping old data is as simple as dropping the old partition — one DDL command that takes milliseconds instead of a DELETE that would have to delete millions of rows one by one and then vacuum the space.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Range Partitioning by Month

```sql
-- Parent table (no data stored here directly)
CREATE TABLE orders (
    id         BIGINT,
    customer_id INT,
    amount     NUMERIC(10,2),
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL
) PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at);

-- Monthly partitions
CREATE TABLE orders_2024_01
    PARTITION OF orders FOR VALUES FROM ('2024-01-01') TO ('2024-02-01');

CREATE TABLE orders_2024_02
    PARTITION OF orders FOR VALUES FROM ('2024-02-01') TO ('2024-03-01');

-- Each partition can have its own indexes
CREATE INDEX ON orders_2024_01 (customer_id);
CREATE INDEX ON orders_2024_02 (customer_id);
```

## Partition Pruning in Action

```sql
-- Query filtered on partition key → only reads jan 2024 partition
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE created_at BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-01-31';
-- Plan: Append → Seq Scan on orders_2024_01 (other partitions excluded)

-- Query without partition key → scans ALL partitions
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 123;  -- scans every month
-- Here a global index on customer_id helps (PostgreSQL 11+)
```

## Archiving Old Data

```sql
-- Drop an old partition (fast, no vacuum needed)
DROP TABLE orders_2022_01;  -- instant, drops the file

-- Detach partition for archival without dropping
ALTER TABLE orders DETACH PARTITION orders_2022_01;
-- Can now archive / compress this table separately
```

## Automate Partition Creation

Use pg_partman extension or a scheduled job:
```sql
-- Create next month's partition before it's needed
CREATE TABLE orders_2025_01
    PARTITION OF orders FOR VALUES FROM ('2025-01-01') TO ('2025-02-01');
```

speakable_v2.hook: Partitioning splits one logical table into multiple physical child tables called partitions, each storing a subset of the data based on a partition key.
speakable_v2.cap: Dropping old data is as simple as dropping the old partition — one DDL command that takes milliseconds instead of a DELETE that would have to delete millions of rows one by one and then.

questions.title: How Database Indexes Work
questions.question: How do database indexes work and how do you decide which columns to index?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **B-tree index: balanced tree, O(log n) lookup — default index type**
- **Index speeds reads but slows writes (insert/update/delete must update index)**
- **Index columns that appear in WHERE, JOIN ON, ORDER BY**
- **Composite index: column order matters — leftmost prefix rule**
- **Covering index: includes all columns the query needs — avoids table lookup**
- **Don't over-index: each index costs write performance and storage**

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
An index is a separate data structure (B-tree by default in most RDBMS) that allows the database to locate rows without scanning the entire table. Without an index, every query does a full table scan — O(n). With a B-tree index, lookup is O(log n). The trade-off: indexes consume disk space and must be updated on every write.

You should index columns that appear frequently in WHERE clauses, JOIN conditions, or ORDER BY clauses on large tables. For composite indexes (multiple columns), the order matters — the database can use the index for queries on the leftmost columns, but not if you skip the first column.

The covering index technique is powerful for read-heavy queries: if you include all the columns a query needs directly in the index, the database never touches the main table — it answers the query entirely from the index.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## B-Tree Index Structure

```
Table: orders (10 million rows)
Columns: id, user_id, status, total, created_at

WITHOUT index on user_id:
  SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42
  → Full table scan: read all 10M rows → slow (seconds)

WITH B-tree index on user_id:
  → B-tree lookup: O(log 10M) ≈ 23 comparisons → fast (milliseconds)

B-Tree structure:
         [500]
        /     \
    [250]      [750]
   /     \    /     \
[100] [375] [600] [900]

Each node stores key values and pointers to child nodes or data rows.
Leaf nodes are linked → range scans are efficient.
```

## When to Index

```sql
-- INDEX THIS: High-cardinality columns in WHERE/JOIN
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_id ON orders(user_id);
-- Cardinality: 1M unique users → index very selective → big win

-- DON'T INDEX THIS: Low-cardinality columns
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_status ON orders(status);
-- Cardinality: only 5 statuses (PENDING, CONFIRMED, etc.)
-- Index returns 20% of rows → full scan might be faster
-- Exception: combine with other high-cardinality columns in composite index

-- INDEX ORDER BY columns on large result sets:
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_created_at ON orders(created_at);
SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;
-- Without index: sort 10M rows → with index: read 20 from sorted structure

-- INDEX JOIN columns:
CREATE INDEX idx_order_items_order_id ON order_items(order_id);
SELECT o.id, i.product_id FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON o.id = i.order_id;
-- order_id is FK — always index FK columns!
```

## Composite Index — Column Order Matters

```sql
-- Composite index: (user_id, status, created_at)
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_status_created ON orders(user_id, status, created_at);

-- Leftmost prefix rule:
-- ✓ Can use index:
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42;                          -- Prefix: user_id
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42 AND status = 'PENDING';  -- Prefix: user_id, status
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42 AND status = 'PENDING'   -- All three
    AND created_at > '2024-01-01';

-- ✗ Cannot use index (skips user_id):
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'PENDING';         -- No user_id → can't use
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE created_at > '2024-01-01'; -- No user_id → can't use

-- Optimize column order: most selective first + matches common query patterns
-- If you always filter by user_id → put it first
-- If most queries filter by user_id + status → (user_id, status) together
```

## Covering Index

```sql
-- Query: get order id and total for a user
SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42;

-- Regular index on user_id:
-- 1. Look up user_id = 42 in index → get row pointers
-- 2. Fetch actual rows from table → read 'id' and 'total'
-- (Two I/O operations: index + table)

-- Covering index includes all needed columns:
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_covering ON orders(user_id, id, total);
-- 1. Look up user_id = 42 in index → directly read id and total from index
-- (One I/O operation: index only — no table access)

-- PostgreSQL: EXPLAIN shows "Index Only Scan" for covering indexes
-- MySQL: EXPLAIN shows "Using index" in Extra column

-- EXPLAIN ANALYZE example:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42;
-- Shows: Index Only Scan using idx_orders_user_covering
--        Rows: 15, actual time: 0.05ms (vs 450ms without index)
```

## Index Impact on Writes

```
Table with 5 indexes:
  idx_user_id
  idx_status
  idx_created_at
  idx_user_status_created (composite)
  idx_user_covering

INSERT into orders:
  → Write row to table
  → Update ALL 5 indexes
  → 6× write operations (1 table + 5 indexes)

UPDATE orders SET status = 'CONFIRMED' WHERE id = 1:
  → Update table row
  → Update idx_status (value changed)
  → Update idx_user_status_created (status changed)
  → 3× write operations

Conclusion:
  - High-write tables: minimize indexes
  - Read-heavy tables: more indexes acceptable
  - Remove unused indexes: query pg_stat_user_indexes / sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats
```

## Production Reality

Always add indexes on foreign key columns (MySQL doesn't do this automatically). Use `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` to verify index usage — sometimes the query planner skips the index if it estimates a full scan is faster (usually correct for small tables or low-cardinality filters). Periodically audit unused indexes using your database's index usage statistics. In PostgreSQL, `pg_stat_user_indexes` shows scan counts — drop indexes with zero scans (in production, over a representative period).
